Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

For a flash fiction piece of this length, it rightly relies primarily on a real-time scene—using sparse dialogue, concrete sensory details (the smell of diesel and wet wood, the muddy suitcase wheels), and physical actions to build quiet tension between the two characters. At the same time, it seamlessly weaves in brief moments of exposition (such as Ilse noting how Jonas used to react in the past, or how the door always sticks when it is damp) to hint at their shared history and establish the setting without interrupting the immediate flow and pacing of their interaction.
